breakfast.name: Firfir (Shredded Injera in Sauce)
ingredients: Optional: scrambled egg or leftover wot (stew)
instructions: Melt niter kibbeh in pan
Sauté onion until soft, add garlic, tomatoes, green chili
Add berbere spice — as much as you like
Tear leftover injera into shreds
Toss injera pieces into the sauce, stir until coated and warmed through
The injera absorbs the spiced butter and sauce — it becomes soft and intensely flavored
Add scrambled egg or leftover wot if desired
Serve on fresh injera — yes, injera on injera, this is Ethiopia
This is how Ethiopians use leftover injera — nothing is wasted
breakfast.description: Ethiopia's waste-nothing breakfast — yesterday's injera torn up and sautéed in spiced butter and berbere sauce. Yes, it's injera served on more injera. The concept of 'leftover bread as breakfast' and the vivid red berbere color make firfir endlessly shareable content.

breakfast.name: Genfo (Ethiopian Porridge)
instructions: Bring water to a boil
Add barley flour gradually, stirring vigorously with a wooden spoon
Stir hard — it should become very thick and smooth, pulling away from the pot
Transfer the mound to a plate, shape into a smooth dome
Make a well in the center
Fill the well with melted niter kibbeh and berbere — it pools like a red-gold volcano
Surround with yogurt
To eat: pull pieces from the edge, dip into the butter-berbere pool
The volcano-of-butter presentation is stunning and viral
breakfast.description: Ethiopian barley porridge shaped into a smooth dome with a crater filled with melted spiced butter and berbere — it looks like a volcano of golden butter in red spice. The dramatic presentation and the dip-and-pull eating technique have made genfo one of East Africa's most viral breakfast foods.

lunch.name: Doro Wot (Chicken Stew)
ingredients: 1 whole chicken (cut into 12 pieces, skin removed)
6 large red onions (finely chopped — NO oil or water for the base)
instructions: Dry-cook the chopped onions — no oil, no water — stir constantly over medium heat until deeply caramelized and reduced by half, 30+ min
This step is non-negotiable and cannot be rushed — the dry-cooked onions are the foundation of all Ethiopian wot
Add niter kibbeh, then berbere, fry until the oil separates and floats
Add garlic, ginger, cardamom
Wash chicken pieces with lemon juice, add to the pot
Simmer covered for 1+ hour until chicken is falling-off-bone tender
Score hard-boiled eggs and nestle into the stew for the last 20 min
The sauce should be thick, deep red, and intensely spiced
Serve on injera — everyone eats from the same platter
This is Ethiopia's Sunday and holiday dish — no celebration happens without doro wot
lunch.description: Ethiopia's queen of stews — chicken slow-cooked in a deep red berbere sauce built on a base of dry-caramelized onions (no oil, no water, just onions and time). The eggs nestled in the sauce and the communal injera platter are the most iconic images of Ethiopian food. The dry-onion technique has gone viral as a universal flavor hack.

lunch.name: Kitfo (Ethiopian Steak Tartare)
ingredients: 500g very fresh lean beef (tenderloin or round), minced by hand
Mitmita spice (hot chili, cardamom, clove, salt)
Ayib (Ethiopian fresh cheese, like dry ricotta)
instructions: The beef must be freshest possible — have the butcher mince it, or hand-mince at home
Warm the niter kibbeh until just melted
Mix minced raw beef with warm niter kibbeh and mitmita spice
Toss gently — the warm butter slightly 'cooks' the exterior of the meat
Serve immediately — traditional is leb leb (very rare, barely warmed) or completely raw
Accompany with ayib cheese and gomen greens
Serve on injera or with kocho
The raw preparation divides people — Ethiopians consider it the pinnacle of their cuisine
You can request it 'derek' (slightly cooked) if raw is too much
lunch.description: Ethiopia's luxurious steak tartare — hand-minced raw beef tossed with warm spiced butter and fiery mitmita chili. Considered the finest dish in Ethiopian cuisine, reserved for special occasions and honored guests. The raw-meat-with-warm-butter technique has made kitfo viral among adventurous food creators worldwide.

lunch.name: Shiro Wot (Chickpea Flour Stew)
ingredients: 1 cup shiro powder (roasted chickpea flour with built-in spices)
instructions: Dry-cook onion (the Ethiopian base technique) until caramelized
Add niter kibbeh, garlic, ginger, tomato
Gradually whisk in shiro powder with water — must be smooth, no lumps
Simmer, stirring, until thick and creamy — 15-20 min
Season with salt, add berbere if you want the spicy version
The consistency should be like thick, smooth hummus when done
Pour onto injera in the center of a shared platter
This is everyday food — the most common Ethiopian meal, especially during fasting seasons
lunch.description: Ethiopia's everyday comfort food — roasted chickpea flour simmered into a thick, creamy, spiced stew. During the 200+ Orthodox fasting days per year, vegan shiro is what most Ethiopians eat daily. The simplicity and the fact that Ethiopian Orthodox fasting created one of the world's oldest vegan cuisines went viral in plant-based food circles.

dinner.name: Tibs (Sautéed Meat)
instructions: Heat niter kibbeh in a pan or clay dish (shekla) very hot
Sear meat on high heat — it must brown, not steam
Add onions, tomatoes, jalapeños
Toss with rosemary, garlic, light berbere
Some versions arrive at your table still sizzling in a clay pot on hot coals
The meat should be browned outside, tender inside
Serve with injera
Tibs is the celebratory sizzle — the sound of meat hitting the hot clay pot is the point
dinner.description: Ethiopia's sizzling meat dish — cubed beef or lamb flash-seared and served in a smoking-hot clay pot (shekla) right at the table. The sizzle when it arrives is theatrical. Tibs videos with the smoking clay pot presentation are some of the most viral Ethiopian food content.

dinner.name: Yebeg Wot (Spiced Lamb Stew)
instructions: Dry-cook onions until deeply caramelized — 30+ min, no shortcuts
Add niter kibbeh, then berbere, fry until oil separates
Add garlic, ginger, cardamom
Add lamb, stir to coat in spice paste
Add water to just cover, bring to simmer
Cook covered 1-1.5 hours until lamb is tender and sauce is thick
The sauce should be reduced, clinging to the meat — not soupy
Serve on a large injera platter for sharing
dinner.description: Slow-braised lamb in a deeply spiced berbere sauce — Ethiopia's richest meat wot. The dry-onion base, the patient braising, and the communal serving style make this a pillar of Ethiopian celebration cooking. The deep red color and fall-apart lamb are irresistible food content.

snacks.name: Sambusa (Ethiopian Samosa)
ingredients: Dough: flour, water, oil, salt (or spring roll wrappers)
Filling: spiced lentils (for fasting) or minced beef with onion, green chili, spices
instructions: Make filling: cook lentils or minced meat with onion, garlic, green chili, cumin, berbere
Let filling cool
Cut dough/wrappers into strips
Fold into triangles, fill, seal edges with water paste
Deep fry at 170°C until golden and crispy — 3-4 min
Drain on paper
Ethiopian sambusas are smaller and spicier than Indian samosas
During fasting, the lentil version is everywhere — an entire parallel vegan street food tradition
snacks.description: Ethiopian samosas — smaller, spicier, and available in both meat and lentil (fasting) versions. The lentil sambusa during Ethiopia's 200+ annual fasting days represents one of the world's oldest plant-based street food traditions, which has gained viral attention in vegan food communities.

snacks.name: Kolo (Roasted Barley and Chickpea Snack)
instructions: Dry-roast barley in a pan until golden and nutty
Dry-roast chickpeas separately until crunchy
Roast peanuts and sunflower seeds
Mix everything together while warm
Season with salt and optional spice
This is Ethiopia's grab-and-go snack — sold in paper cones on every street
Also the traditional snack served during the coffee ceremony
The crunch is addictive — each component has a different texture
snacks.description: Ethiopia's ancient trail mix — roasted barley, chickpeas, peanuts, and sunflower seeds served in paper cones. The original protein snack, eaten for thousands of years and served during Ethiopia's famous coffee ceremony. The simplicity and crunch have earned kolo viral attention as the 'original energy snack.'

desserts.name: Himbasha (Celebration Bread)
instructions: Mix flour, sugar, yeast, spices
Add eggs, milk, melted butter — knead until smooth and elastic
Let rise 1 hour until doubled
Shape into a round loaf
Score a decorative sunburst or spoke pattern on top — this is the signature look
Brush with egg wash
Bake at 175°C for 25-30 min until golden and hollow-sounding
The scoring pattern varies by region and occasion — it's both decorative and functional
Serve at holidays, weddings, and celebrations — never an ordinary Tuesday
desserts.description: Ethiopia's celebration bread — a sweet, cardamom-scented round loaf scored with a beautiful sunburst pattern. Served at weddings, holidays, and every important milestone. The decorative scoring technique and the aromatic cardamom make himbasha a viral symbol of Ethiopian hospitality.

drinks.name: Ethiopian Coffee Ceremony (Buna)
ingredients: Green coffee beans (Ethiopian-grown: Yirgacheffe, Sidamo, or Harrar)
instructions: Wash green beans, then roast in a flat pan over charcoal — the aroma fills the room
This is the ceremony: guests smell the roasting beans as they're waved under their noses
Grind roasted beans with mortar and pestle
Boil water in the jebena (clay pot)
Add ground coffee to the jebena, let it brew
Pour from a height into tiny sini cups — the pour is an art
Serve with sugar (no milk traditionally) and popcorn or kolo on the side
Three rounds are served: abol (first), tona (second), baraka (third/blessing)
Declining before the third cup is impolite — it's the blessing round
The entire ceremony takes 1-2 hours — it's a social ritual, not just coffee
drinks.description: Ethiopia invented coffee — and the buna ceremony is the world's most elaborate coffee ritual. Green beans roasted before guests, brewed in a clay jebena, poured from height into tiny cups, served three rounds with popcorn and incense. The ceremony has become viral as the original 'coffee culture,' predating every café on Earth by centuries.
